metadata.title: How Does Claude Prep for a Due Diligence Meeting?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude draws on its own instinct to decide what to ask in a due diligence meeting -- or is doing something narrower. Lands the carry-out that the prep turns the meeting type into a question list, benchmarks, and red flags from a written file, and only covers meeting types the file defines.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carries real skill-specific facts (not unfilled template placeholders) -- see QUESTION.md. Facts preserved: the dd-meeting-prep skill prepares for due diligence meetings -- management presentations, expert network calls, customer references, and advisor sessions; generates targeted question lists, benchmarks to reference, and red flags to probe; used before any diligence meeting or call. Register re-registered Teardown -> Plain; source's B03 design-tell verdict became a plain mechanism + both-directions beat; a wrong-guess beat and an anchor (an expert network call about a staffing company: a 'same-store margin trend' question drafted -> benchmarked -> asked -> flagged) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure, since the source's Teardown shape carried neither.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (an expert network call about a staffing company: 'same-store margin trend' drafted -> benchmarked -> asked -> flagged as a red flag, then paid off into 'run twice, same questions' / 'a meeting type outside the file has nothing tailored to reach for')

beats.narration_text: Someone asks whether Claude walks into a diligence call and just knows the sharp questions to ask — pattern-matching on some private well of deal instinct. It doesn't do that. What's actually happening is smaller than that, and more useful. Liam here, in for Bear. Let's take it apart.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What decides the questions -- instinct?', hesitates on 'instinct', corrects to 'the file', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('instinct' -> 'the file') is visible on a late frame, fully settled before the beat ends.

beats.narration_text: Here's the natural guess. Claude has read a lot of finance and picked up something like a deal person's reflex, so on the call it improvises the questions an experienced partner would ask. That is not the mechanism. What the skill actually does is check which meeting type you're prepping — a management presentation, an expert network call, a customer reference, or an advisor session — and reach for the prepared machinery for that one type: the question list, the benchmarks to reference, the red flags to probe. Those four types are what the file describes. Feed it a meeting outside that list and it has nothing tailored to reach for. That's the trade-off in one line: they optimized for coverage inside four defined meeting types at the cost of any coverage outside them.

shot.new_visual_element: An 'instinct' figure with a scattered thought-bubble, struck through; a meeting-type-to-outputs procedure card lit instead

production_viz.label: Instinct, struck -- meeting type, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'INSTINCT' beside a thought-bubble of scattered decision marks. Right: a numbered card labelled 'MEETING TYPE -> QUESTIONS + BENCHMARKS + FLAGS' listing three steps: read the meeting type, match its template, build the question list. The instinct side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the procedure side stays lit. A final line reads 'meeting type not listed -- no template' and the figure does not reach for it.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening, step by step. Match the meeting type to its template. Generate the question list. Attach the benchmark each question is measured against. Mark the red flags to probe if the answer drifts. Watch the anchor: an expert network call about a staffing company. One question — same-store margin trend — gets drafted from the template, gets a peer benchmark attached, gets asked live on the call, and comes back flagged because the expert's answer leans on one large client. The value isn't a smarter question. The value is that this exact question gets built, benchmarked, asked, and evaluated every time this meeting type comes up.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a 'same-store margin' question traveling drafted -> benchmarked -> asked -> flagged

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one question, four stops
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four stacked cards labelled 'DRAFTED', 'BENCHMARKED', 'ASKED', 'FLAGGED'. A single highlighted token 'SAME-STORE MARGIN' travels down through all four cards in turn, each lighting terracotta as it arrives. At the bottom, beside the FLAGGED card, a small note reads 'leans on one large client' and the token halts there. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, CONDENSED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That flag surfaces because the question was built to probe for exactly that kind of concentration risk — the template escalates what it already watches for; it doesn't go hunting past its edge. And it holds in both directions. Prep the same expert-network call twice and the question list, benchmarks, and red flags come back identical — that's the design paying off; you get repeatability, not creativity. Ask it to prep a regulator sit-down instead and there's nothing tailored to reach for; the prep stops exactly where SKILL.md does. This works if you value repeatable prep on defined meeting types; it fails if you need improvisation on a meeting the file never saw.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS, condensed; splits into 'run twice -- same questions' and 'regulator sit-down -- no template'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- run twice, or stops there
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 COMPOSITION RETURNS, condensed to a small resting row (BENCHMARKED / ASKED / FLAGGED). It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'RUN TWICE' then 'SAME QUESTIONS' with a checkmark, labelled 'same input, same questions' (holds); right reads 'REGULATOR SIT-DOWN' then a struck-through 'TAILORED?', labelled 'stops where the file does' (flips).

beats.narration_text: A Claude due-diligence meeting prep isn't insider instinct about what to ask. It's a written procedure that turns the meeting type into a question list, the benchmarks to reference, and the red flags to probe — and it only covers meeting types the file defines.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Tell me you're prepping for an expert network call on a staffing company, and run the dd-meeting-prep skill: build the question list, the benchmarks it attaches, and the red flags it would probe for. Then ask it to prep a meeting type you've never mentioned supporting, and watch whether new questions get invented or the prep stops where the file does. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Tell me you're prepping for an expert network call on a staffing company, and run the dd-meeting-prep skill: build the question list, the benchmarks it attaches, and the red flags it would probe for. Then ask for a meeting type I've never mentioned supporting.

beats.narration_text: One more, without the skill. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — it'll do a rougher version of what the skill does, using nothing but the model. Tell it the meeting type and who you're meeting; ask it for the questions, the industry benchmark each question is measured against, and the red flags in the answers that mean dig deeper. Then read it back — you'll see where a template beats improvisation, and where it doesn't. Go deeper: which of those questions actually falsify a bull case on the target, and which only give it more ways to confirm itself?

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm prepping for an [expert network call] with [a former operator at a mid-market staffing company we're evaluating for acquisition]. Act as a due-diligence analyst. Give me: (1) 8–10 targeted questions with the specific risk each one is probing for; (2) the industry or peer benchmark each answer should be compared against; (3) 3–5 red flags in the answers that would tell me to dig further before committing. Group them by theme. Plain text, no marketing tone.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: which of those questions actually falsify a bull case on the target, and which only give the target more ways to confirm it? Rewrite the list so at least half the questions are the falsifying kind.
